item.title: Democrats seize control of Congress after flipping House and Senate
item.description:
Democrats have regained control of Congress, winning back the U.S. House and Senate as Republican midterm losses mount.

Coming into the night, Republicans held 53 of the Senate's 100 seats, compared with 45 held by Democrats. To wrest back control of the Senate, Democrats needed a net gain of at least four seats. Before the clock struck midnight on the East Coast, the Associated Press said the party would gain at least that amount.

Democrats won a series of key Senate seats. In Michigan, Abdul El-Sayed defeated Mike Rogers in one of the most closely watched races. James Talarico beat Republican Ken Paxton in Texas, becoming the first Democrat to win a U.S. Senate seat in the Lone Star State since 1988. 

Annie Andrews beat GOP Sen. Darline Graham in South Carolina to flip a Senate seat. In Maine, Democrat Troy Jackson defeated incumbent GOP Sen. Susan Collins, putting an end to her three-decade tenure. Sen. Jon Ossoff comfortably won reelection in Georgia. Other Senate seats to flip to the Democratic Party included Roy Cooper in North Carolina and Sherrod Brown in Ohio.

In the 435-seat House, the GOP held 218 seats, compared with 214 held by Democrats. To retake control of the House, Democrats needed a net gain of three seats — and the AP said early Wednesday that the party had exceeded that figure.

There were also 36 gubernatorial races and numerous ballot measures to keep an eye on. Democrat Keisha Lance Bottoms of Georgia became the first Black woman elected governor in U.S. history, while Democrat Amy Acton became the first woman elected governor of Ohio. In Florida, Republican Byron Donalds became the state's first Black governor-elect.

President Trump, whose approval ratings are at or near all-time lows, distanced himself from mounting Republican losses in a post on Truth Social on Tuesday night, "I wasn't on the Ballot and if I was, we would have won IN A LANDSLIDE!" Trump wrote. "Thank you for your attention to this matter."

This article originally appeared on Yahoo News at https://www.yahoo.com/news/politics/live/midterms-2026-live-updates-election-day-voters-head-to-the-polls-as-democrats-look-to-flip-gop-control-of-the-house-and-senate-110000715.html

item.title: Democrats' blue wave became a tsunami. The shift went far beyond swing states.
item.description:
It was a blue wave big enough to become a blue tsunami.

On Tuesday, the Democratic Party shattered a series of decades-long Republican winning streaks, notched several historic firsts and flipped both the U.S. Senate and House of Representatives as Americans in states and districts that voted to reelect President Trump just two years ago delivered a harsh judgment on the steep tariffs, rising gas prices, aggressive immigration raids and unresolved war in Iran that have so far dominated his second term.

"We didn't win this race by alienating our neighbors or shaming our neighbors or ridiculing our neighbors," Democrat James Talarico said after winning the Senate election in Texas. "We embodied a new kind of politics. A politics rooted in a deep love for our state, for our country and, most importantly, for all of our neighbors."

Votes were still being tallied and key races remained uncalled as Election Day came to an end. But as of 1 a.m. ET on Wednesday, when the last polls closed in Alaska, Democrats were projected to gain more than three dozen seats in the House and as many as nine seats in the Senate — far beyond the three and four seats, respectively, that they needed to retake each chamber. They were also on track to win the majority of governorships for the first time since 2011.

The list of milestones was long: The first Texas Democrat elected to the U.S. Senate since 1988 (Talarico). The first Latina ever elected governor of the Lone Star State (Gina Hinojosa). Kansas's first Democratic senator since the Great Depression (Adam Hamilton). The first Black woman governor in U.S. history (Georgia's Keisha Lance Bottoms). The first Democratic senator from South Carolina in decades (Annie Andrews). America's first Muslim senator (Abdul El-Sayed of Michigan). And what could be the largest Democratic House majority since 2008.

As a result, Trump will no longer enjoy complete Republican control of Congress. Starting in January, Democrats in the House and Senate will have the power to block parts of the president's agenda, reject his nominees, investigate his administration and even impeach him (again). 

Historically, midterms tend to be backlash elections; a president's party almost always sheds House seats when voters return to the polls to rate his first two years in office. The average number lost since World War II? Twenty-six.

Yet some midterms are more momentous than others. In 2006, President George W. Bush's second midterm, Republicans lost 31 seats. In 2010, President Barack Obama's first midterm, Democrats lost 64 seats. And in 2018, Trump's first midterm, Republicans lost 42 seats.

This year, according to data journalist G. Elliott Morris, "Democrats have won the largest House popular vote victory for any party since 1974, when the Watergate scandal rocked Republicans to their core." 

Here are four takeaways that help explain what happened in the 2026 midterms, and why.

Red state revolt

The most striking thing about this year's Democratic gains is that they came in some of the redder parts of the country. 

Before Election Day, the GOP's majorities on Capitol Hill were already narrow — a dynamic that usually limits the opposing party's pickup opportunities. A Republican-friendly 2026 Senate map and an unprecedented mid-decade GOP redistricting push further reduced the number of easy targets for Democrats. 

Yet high prices, an unpopular war and Trump's falling approval ratings gave Democrats a chance to compete in places where they haven't prevailed in years — or, in some cases, decades. 

Strong nominees went on to capitalize Tuesday night.

In Texas, Talarico, a 37-year-old state lawmaker and former seminarian, defeated Republican Attorney General Ken Paxton, a MAGA favorite with a controversial past. In Kansas, Hamilton, a 61-year-old megachurch pastor and former Republican, defeated incumbent GOP Sen. Roger Marshall. In Iowa, Democrat Josh Turek, a state lawmaker and two-time Paralympic gold medalist who describes himself as a "prairie populist," defeated GOP Rep. Ashley Hinson, a former local news anchor. In South Carolina, Andrews, a pediatrician, defeated incumbent Sen. Darline Graham, who was appointed to the seat after the recent death of her brother, longtime Sen. Lindsey Graham. In Ohio, Democrat Sherrod Brown defeated incumbent Republican Sen. Jon Husted to book a return ticket to the U.S. Senate, where he previously served from 2007 to 2025. 

Democrat Scott Colom was even leading incumbent Republican Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith in Mississippi by a handful of votes. 

These are not the types of races Democrats typically win. Trump won Ohio by 11 points in 2024. He won Iowa by 13 points. He won Texas by 14. He won Kansas by 16. He won South Carolina by 18. He won Mississippi by 24. He won North Carolina — where former Democratic Gov. Roy Cooper breezed to victory — by 3.

Whether the 2026 results foreshadow some sort of larger rural realignment — or just a temporary rebuke of Trump's current policies — remains to be seen. But either way, Tuesday's blue tsunami swept well into red America.

The Trump effect

Before Election Day, the president urged his supporters to vote like he was on the ballot. Afterward, he wrote on social media, "I wasn't on the Ballot and if I was, we would have won IN A LANDSLIDE!"

But preliminary exit polls suggested that even if Americans couldn't technically cast their votes for — or against — Trump this time around, his performance and policies were very much top of mind. 

A full 62% of midterm voters said they disapproved of how Trump is handling his job as president. Just 38% said they approved. No recent president has emerged from a midterm election with an approval rating that low. Nearly 90% of voters said the cost of living was a crucial or major factor in their vote; about the same number said they were concerned about the price of gas and groceries. Nearly two-thirds said that Trump's policies, including tariffs, have made the U.S. economy worse and that going to war with Iran was the wrong decision. More than half said Trump is not a strong leader, does not fight for people like them, does not have the right priorities and does not have the mental capability to serve effectively as president.

Meanwhile, Trump did little to boost Republican chances on Election Day. His endorsements and interventions appeared to backfire in contest after contest. He attracted more attention in the closing days of the campaign for praising certain candidates' anatomy than for promoting his party's agenda. And he spent his final appearance before Nov. 3 talking about his troubled reflecting pool project.

Trump has defied history before. But in the end, 2026 seemed to show that even his powers have their limits. In 2006, President George W. Bush's Republicans lost both the House and the Senate after Americans soured on another Middle Eastern war. Something similar happened again on Tuesday.  

Swing voters swung — hard 

The big story of the 2024 presidential election was how a rightward shift among previously left-leaning independents and Latinos helped propel Trump back to the presidency. 

It appears both groups have shifted back. 

According to Equis, a polling firm that focuses on Latino voters, Democrats increased their overall share of the Latino vote by 10 points in 2026 (65%) compared to 2024 (55%). In some states, like Virginia (+19 points) and New Jersey (+23 points), Democratic gains among Latinos were even bigger. In others, like Texas (60%) and Florida (56%), Democrats went from losing the Latino vote last time to winning it. Those gains likely contributed to key House victories in both states and major statewide wins in Texas. 

As for self-identified independents, Trump split them about evenly with Democrat Kamala Harris two years ago. This time around, independents appear to have favored Democrats by roughly 17 percentage points. 

A new generation of Democrats 

For decades, Democrats have lamented their party's gerontocracy, from the Silent Generation stalwarts who long led their congressional caucus to the baby boomer candidates who seem to keep winning their presidential nominations. 

But Tuesday's tsunami has provided the party with a whole new batch of "elder Millennial" stars, including Talarico (37), El-Sayed (42), Andrews (45), Turek (47), Iowa Gov.-elect Rob Sand (44) and Georgia Sen. Jon Ossoff (39), whose cruise to reelection has inspired buzz about a possible presidential bid (which he has publicly ruled out).

Before Nov. 3, former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg, New York Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez and New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani were among the most prominent Democrats representing the party's next generation on the national stage. Now they have company.

item.title: Democrat Abdul El-Sayed wins historic Senate race in Michigan
item.description:
Democrat Abdul El-Sayed has won one of the marquee battles of the 2026 midterms: the race to succeed retiring Democratic Sen. Gary Peters in Michigan.

El-Sayed, an unapologetic 42-year-old progressive and the son of Egyptian immigrants, will become America's first Muslim senator. He has pushed policies such as Medicare for All and ending U.S. military aid to Israel, and has been willing to confront his critics and his own party's establishment.

His victory over Republican candidate Mike Rogers came on a night that saw Democrats regain control of the U.S. Senate in a midterm blue wave that also saw the party win control of the House of Representatives.

"You took a chance on the unlikeliest of candidates," El-Sayed told a crowd of supporters in Detroit on Wednesday as he declared victory. "Thank you. This is all yours."

El-Sayed defeated Rogers, a 63-year-old former congressman who lost an extremely close Senate race to Democratic Sen. Elissa Slotkin two years ago, and who has since broken with President Trump on tariffs and the war in Iran.

The race was rocked by several controversies, with the biggest coming two days before the election. Rep. Haley Stevens, the Democrat El-Sayed narrowly defeated in the primary, endorsed Rogers after she worshipped with the GOP candidate at Perfecting Church in Detroit.

"Our Democratic nominee for Senate said I was no longer welcome in his campaign and that I should stay away," Stevens said in a video. "And he's right. And that's why I am endorsing Mike Rogers for the United States Senate today."

Stevens had said days earlier that she would vote for El-Sayed, and the two were due to appear together Sunday for the first time since August. That plan collapsed after she called on him to condemn an outside group's ad tying U.S. support for Israel to grocery prices. His campaign then asked her to stay away, NBC News reported. El-Sayed has stated he did not agree with the contents of the ad.

Defending her stance, Stevens told CNN on Sunday the decision was a "weight off my shoulders" and said she had decided to switch allegiances because El-Sayed had been getting "angrier and angrier" throughout the campaign.

When Stevens announced her change in support for Rogers, she maintained that she was "still a very proud Democrat." Michigan's Democratic Party chair, Curtis Hertel, fumed over the decision in a Sunday post on X, writing, "Congresswoman Stevens is not a current member of the Michigan Democratic Party, nor will she be in the future."

Trump told a rally in Iowa on Sunday that he'd "love" Stevens to join the Republican Party and said she'd been "very brave" to endorse Rogers.

Rep. Debbie Dingell, who helped arrange the event, told the AP before the endorsement that she had called it off. "I'm the one who pulled it because it had become way too distracting," she said.

"I would rather not distract from the key issues of this campaign," El-Sayed said Saturday. He attended a different Detroit church Sunday with Dingell and other Democrats, and did not address the dispute there, the AP reported.

On Sunday, El-Sayed spoke with reporters before a unity event with other Democrats and reacted to Stevens's endorsement, saying, "At the end of the day, I actually don't think about Haley Stevens."

"This is a state of 10 million people who deserve a lot better from their government. I'm a lot more focused on the 9,999,998 that are not the ones you guys are talking about," El-Sayed said, referring to Stevens and Rogers.

Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer wrote on social media on Sunday that Stevens's reversal was a "despicable betrayal."

How controversial has the race been? 

El-Sayed's background has made him the target of persistent attacks from Republicans, with Trump going so far as to call him a "jihadist" and accuse him of being "on the side of the terrorists." 

Vice President JD Vance recently said El-Sayed had "zero attachment" to the United States. El-Sayed is a U.S. citizen who was born and raised in Michigan. Rogers has claimed, without evidence, that El-Sayed has supported the Muslim Brotherhood, one of the Arab world's oldest and most influential Islamist groups.

In a recent exchange at a town hall with a critic who asked him whether he denounced the Muslim Brotherhood, El-Sayed highlighted what he called the "implicit" suggestion in the question: the assumption that he'll have "dual loyalties" because of his faith. 

"I'm not running to be a Muslim senator," he said. "I'm running for the U.S. Senate and happen to be Muslim."

After Trump referred to El-Sayed as "Mohammed" — his middle name — the Democrat responded in what has become his signature pugnacious style. 

"I don't care how he pronounces my name," El-Sayed said during a rally in Grand Rapids on Oct. 25. "Because he can just go on and call me 'senator' after November. I will be Senator Mohamed to you, bro."

Meanwhile, El-Sayed has campaigned with Hasan Piker, a Marxist streamer whom other Democrats have called antisemitic and even anti-American. 

"If perfectly inoffensive won elections, then Donald Trump would never have been president," El-Sayed said in April when reporters questioned his choice of allies. 

An independent left-wing group affiliated with Piker's uncle, commentator Cenk Uygur, also recently released an ad linking U.S. support for Israel to high grocery prices. The ad shows two parents shopping for their kids' lunch items; the mom tells the dad to put a carton of eggs back on the shelf. 

"They don't like eggs anymore?" the dad asks.

"No, they like eggs," the mom answers. "But we have to set that $7 aside for killing Palestinians."

Some Democrats and Republicans have urged El-Sayed to denounce the content of the ad rather than just distancing himself from it. 

"That has nothing to do with our campaign," El-Sayed said of the ad. "It's certainly not what I want to be talking about right now."

Who is El-Sayed? 

El-Sayed, 42, was born on Halloween 1984 in Rochester Hills, Mich. — a northern suburb of Detroit. His parents were immigrants from Egypt, and his first language was Arabic. He captained his high school's wrestling, football and lacrosse teams, then continued to play club lacrosse at the University of Michigan, where he majored in biology and political science. 

El-Sayed went on to study medicine at Michigan, Oxford University (as a Rhodes Scholar) and Columbia University, where he received his MD. Before politics, he pursued a career in public health epidemiology as a tenure-track professor, and later led the Detroit health department. 

In 2017, El-Sayed, then just 32, resigned as Detroit's health director to run for governor. He said at the time he was inspired by his work on the Flint water crisis. He was endorsed by prominent progressives — Bernie Sanders and Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez — but lost the Democratic primary to Gretchen Whitmer by more than 20 percentage points.

After a stint as Wayne County health director, El-Sayed decided to try again in 2026. He has since become the most prominent Democratic insurgent to channel left-wing disillusionment with politics and outrage over Israel's actions in Gaza to win his party's nomination in a state where more moderate candidates typically prevail. His argument is that even in so-called purple states such as Michigan, Democrats have a better shot at success when they pick buzzy, big-swing progressives over safe, "electable" incrementalists.

item.title: Elon Musk jokes about GOP election defeat after spending record amount on party
item.description:
Tech billionaire Elon Musk joked on Wednesday about Republicans' defeat in US midterm elections after spending hundreds of millions of dollars to help the party.

Democrats seized control of the US Congress on Tuesday, capturing both the Senate and House of Representatives in a stunning rejection of President Donald Trump's political agenda.

"Guess my election-interfering space lasers didn't work this time," Musk said on X, including the shrug emoji.

Musk contributed nearly half a billion dollars to Republican political efforts, making him the largest individual contributor in a federal election cycle since unlimited election spending was allowed in 2010, according to campaign finance tracker OpenSecrets.

His donations have mostly gone to his Republican-leaning America PAC, as well as to the Republican Senate Leadership Fund (SLF) super PAC.

The SLF used Musk's $158 million in donations in September to support Ken Paxton, the Republican Senate candidate in Texas.

The Texas Senate election topped the list in terms of expenditure, with Paxton's Democrat challenger James Talarico facing more than $200 million in opposition from outside spending groups.

Talarico defeated Paxton, a close ally of Trump, to become the first Democrat to win statewide office in Texas since 1994. 

He took aim at Musk at a victory rally in Austin. 

"In this race, we went up against our own Goliaths. The richest man in the world, the most powerful man in the world and the entire Washington, DC establishment," Talarico said.

He also targeted billionaires "who own the social media algorithms, who own the cable news networks, who own the politicians fighting on our screens" and who "want us at each other's throats."

- 'Billionaire's world' -

Democrat Gina Hinojosa unseated incumbent Texas Governor Greg Abbott in another blow to the deeply conservative southern border state.

Hinojosa said she asked at the start of her campaign if Texas was "a state that is by and for the people of Texas."

"Or is this the billionaire's world and we just live here? Does Texas belong to the parents and their children? Or the billionaires trying to dismantle our schools? Does Texas belong to the farmers and ranchers who have worked this land for generations? Or the corporations trying to buy it up?" she said after her victory. 

Talarico and Hinojosa both campaigned on tighter regulations for AI data centers. 

The spread of data centers across Texas has become a central issue as residents worry about rising electricity bills, water use and strain on the power grid.

Musk has moved the headquarters of his comapanies Tesla, SpaceX and X to Texas.

"Data centers in space looking pretty appealing right now," Musk joked on X after the result. 

The Supreme Court ruled in 2010 that the government cannot limit political spending by corporations, unions and other groups if they spend it independently of candidates.

A lower court decision ruled that these organizations could also raise an unlimited amount of money from donors.

Now, big donors can allocate vast sums of money to try to influence elections and remain anonymous by donating through secondary organizations.

Spending sprees by donors have surged under Trump's administration, with Musk's large donations encapsulating the new reality of pay-to-play politics.

item.title: Supermarket fridges are being hacked across Europe, and the damage is in the millions
item.description:
LONDON (AP) — Mysterious cyberattacks on European supermarket fridges have sent officials around the continent scrambling to figure out the cold, hard facts.

Supermarkets in a number of European countries reported this week that their fridges and freezers warmed up after they were remotely taken over, resulting in tons of spoiled food at a total cost of millions of dollars (euros).

One Swedish supermarket said its fridges and freezers had been hacked and set to 50 degrees Celsius (122 degrees Fahrenheit).

It's a repeat of an earlier incident that struck refrigeration systems in hundreds of supermarkets and independent stores across France, Belgium and the Netherlands.

Here's a closer look:

What happened and who was affected

Supermarkets in at least half a dozen European countries, including Sweden, Belgium, Luxembourg, Ireland, Italy and Estonia, reported problems on Monday.

It wasn't just big chains.

The owner of a butcher shop in Athens told private Greek Skai TV Tuesday that someone hacked into the temperature control of a refrigeration unit, raising the temperature to 150 degrees Celsius (302 degrees Fahrenheit).

George Boubas said his employees who start their shift at 4 a.m. at the shop in the Kifisia suburb first noticed the problem. It took a technician two hours to wrest back control of the unit’s temperature settings, although the meat products weren’t affected, he said.

Boubas said the technician told him that an area supermarket and a fast-food restaurant experienced the same issue.

He said they resorted to switching off the Wi-Fi connection to the refrigeration units to restrict outside access.

Experts said the cyberattacks were a reminder of the risks that come as more things get connected to the internet.

“This attack is a wake-up call. We have filled our homes and shops with devices that are really small computers, yet we still treat them like ordinary appliances," said Katerina Mitrokotsa, a cybersecurity professor at the University of St. Gallen, in Switzerland.

“A fridge doesn’t look like a security risk, and that’s exactly why attackers like it.”

Fridges are connected to save money and cut waste

The cyberattack mirrors one that happened weeks earlier that affected mainly French and Dutch retailers.

French cybersecurity investigators blamed problems with outdated remote control modules made by Danish company Danfoss as well as U.S.-based Copeland. Danfoss said most affected systems were older products that no longer received software or security updates, while Copeland identified a vulnerability in discontinued controllers.

“Supermarkets connect their fridges so they can monitor temperatures around the clock across hundreds of stores, get alerts before food spoils, cut energy costs and let technicians fix faults remotely," Mitrokotsa said.

"This saves money and reduces food waste, but every connected fridge is also an entry point that needs to be secured like any other IT system.”

Experts said many businesses are rushing to embrace trendy new technology while neglecting the vast network of connections that they rely on for their daily operations, from payment and ordering systems to warehouses, refrigeration and other building controls.

“Organizations are pouring budget into AI and digital transformation while the systems that keep food cold, water clean, and lights on often run on hardware that has not been funded since installation," said Nicole Carignan, senior vice president of security and AI strategy at cybersecurity company Darktrace.

“Nobody broke into these refrigeration systems with a zero-day," she said, using a term for a flaw that has gone undetected by the system’s creators and security reviews. "They got in through internet-facing controllers, end-of-life firmware, and default passwords. That is technical debt coming due.”

British cybersecurity officials on Tuesday shed little light on the latest attack, while pointing to what they called “legacy technology.”

“The cyberattack on French supermarkets was a result of exploitation of known vulnerabilities,” U.K. cyber minister Liz Lloyd said in a speech. “It’s a clear demonstration that poor cyber hygiene, like weak passwords, continues to put organizations at risk.”

Richard Horne, the head of the U.K.’s National Cyber Security Center, told reporters the French fridges were "connected directly to the internet with default passwords.”

A team from the center issued warnings and worked through Monday night contacting organizations that had “vulnerable technology exposed,” he said.

No evidence so far that AI was involved

Advanced artificial intelligence systems from companies like Anthropic and OpenAI have come under fire recently after a string of revelations that they hacked into organizations while evading human control.

Experts, however, said Tuesday that they didn't think these attacks were powered by AI.

“There is no evidence AI was used, and the techniques did not require it,” said Carignan.

“I think the key element of that is that this wasn’t an AI attack” said Paul Chichester, director of operations at the U.K. cyber center. “This is using vulnerabilities that absolutely have been out there for a long period of time. And that’s where we really need to sort of focus on.”

Who’s behind it and what's the motive

Investigations have so far failed to discover who might have carried out the cyberattacks and why.

France’s national cybersecurity agency, ANSSI, said it has been investigating refrigeration-system breaches since mid-October and coordinating protective measures with “all sectors that could be affected.”

In a statement to The Associated Press, the agency said it knew of compromised remote refrigeration controllers in Danfoss’s AK-SM and AK-SC ranges, as well as Copeland and Dixell xweb systems.

ANSSI said it was mobilized to assist “potential victims in France” and pointed to a security alert first published Oct. 12, which has been updated regularly.

Italian cybersecurity and intelligence officials were scheduled to meet Tuesday morning to discuss the incident, according to Italian news agency ANSA.

Officials at the European Union's executive Commission were also holding similar meetings.

European Commission spokesperson Thomas Regnier declined on Tuesday to comment on who might have carried out the hacks, saying that's up to the bloc's 27 national authorities to figure out.

Regnier told reporters the incidents “are not isolated” and that Europeans "have to be collectively resilient and prepared for such cyber incidents.”

___

Hadjicostis reported from Nicosia, Cyprus. AP writers Lorne Cook in Brussels, Lefteris Pitarakis in Athens and Thomas Adamson in Paris contributed to this report.

item.title: 8 candidates who made history in the 2026 midterm elections
item.description:
The 2026 midterm elections made history for several candidates, as voters are projected to have elected the country's first Black, Native American and Latina female governors and more major firsts.

All eyes were on the results Tuesday night in the high-stakes election, in which House and Senate races will determine the balance of power in Congress.

But the midterms have also seen an expansion of representation among America's lawmakers, with several candidates celebrating groundbreaking wins.

This story will be updated as more wins are projected.

Keisha Lance Bottoms

Democratic candidate Keisha Lance Bottoms is projected by ABC News to become the next governor of Georgia -- beating billionaire Rick Jackson in the closely watched race.

The projected win for Bottoms, the former mayor of Atlanta, flips the Georgia governor's mansion blue in a state that President Donald Trump won in 2024.

In the closing stretch of the race, Bottoms often repeated on the campaign trail that Jackson "may have the money, but the people still have the power." Before the end of the cycle, Jackson had spent more than $200 million of his personal fortune on his campaign.

Georgia hasn't elected a Democrat for governor since 1998. The seat is currently held by Republican Gov. Brian Kemp, who was term-limited this year.

This is a major win for Georgia Democrats, who have targeted this seat for years, falling short in 2018 and 2022 with Democrat Stacey Abrams. In 2018, Abrams lost to Kemp by a 1.4-point margin.

Deb Haaland

Deb Haaland, the former U.S. Secretary of the Interior, is projected to win New Mexico's gubernatorial race, becoming the first indigenous governor in U.S. history.

"Thank you, New Mexico! It is the honor of my lifetime to be elected your 33rd Governor," Haaland wrote on X. "Tonight, you made history. You chose a future where New Mexico comes first, where working families have a chance to get ahead, and where every New Mexican has a voice."

She is a member of the Laguna Pueblo, a federally recognized tribe in the state.

Haaland's projected win on Tuesday was against former Rio Rancho Mayor Gregg Hull.

In 2018, Haaland became one of the first two Native women elected to Congress.

"In 230 years, there's never been a Native American woman in Congress. I have never seen myself in that body of our government," Haaland said in an interview with ABC News at the time.

Rep. Gina Hinojosa

The Texas gubernatorial race is also projected to see a historic first, with Democratic Rep. Gina Hinojosa becoming the state's first Latina governor.

Hinojosa was running against Republican Gov. Greg Abbott, who was aiming to win his fourth term.

The stunning projected win for Hinojosa, who served in the Texas state House, comes after running on education reform and criticizing Abbott over AI data centers.

"This is our last best chance to take back Texas for the people," she wrote on X ahead of the election.

Rep. Byron Donalds

Republican Rep. Byron Donalds is projected by ABC News to win the gubernatorial race in Florida, becoming the state's first Black governor.

"I am humbled and grateful beyond measure," Donalds said in a victory statement posted to X. "As your Governor, I will give you everything I have. We are going to make life in Florida more affordable. We are going to keep our streets safe. We are going to invest in our young people so that they can attain the Florida Dream that all of us love so dearly."

His campaign made headlines in September when Donalds' website was updated to remove some prominent references to Trump. According to the Miami Herald, Donalds removed at least eight references to Trump from his website.

Shortly after the changes, however, Donalds posted a statement on X touting his endorsement of the president.

"I am proud to have President Trump's endorsement. While everyone is focused on our website, check out our policy proposals to make life more affordable for Floridians," Donalds wrote at the time.

Dr. Amy Acton

Dr. Amy Acton, the former director of the Ohio Department of Health, is projected to defeat GOP opponent Vivek Ramaswamy for the Ohio governor's seat.

Acton will become the first woman elected governor in Ohio and the first Jewish governor in the state's history.

The defining moment of this campaign came with an ad made by the Ramaswamy campaign that tried to use Acton's estranged mother, who fled the state with a husband who was indicted for raping Acton as a child, to call Acton a liar. The ad prompted major backlash and an influx of support and visibility for Acton.

David Crowley 

In battleground Wisconsin, Democrat David Crowley, the Milwaukee County executive, will win and become the state's first Black governor, ABC News projects.

Crowley defeated Tom Tiffany, a Trump ally, for the open seat to succeed outgoing Democratic Gov. Tony Evers. A former state lawmaker, Crowley campaigned on his background running the state's largest county and fended off attacks from his Republican opponent, who cast him as weak on crime and immigration.

Crowley campaigned on reducing the cost of living and rejecting "MAGA extremism."

"Thank you, Wisconsin. Thank you for believing in me," he wrote in a statement on X Tuesday night. "Serving as your governor will be the honor of a lifetime."

Democrats pinned their hopes on Crowley to win a state government trifecta for the first time in over a decade in the swing state.

Rep. Chris Pappas

In New Hampshire, ABC News projects that U.S. Rep. Chris Pappas will win the Senate race, becoming the first openly gay senator.

He is projected to beat former Sen. John Sununu, a Republican backed by President Donald Trump, in the race that was seen as a must-hold for the Democrats.

Pappas campaigned with major Democratic figures such as former Vice President Kamala Harris and California Gov. Gavin Newsom.

Dr. Abdul El-Sayed

ABC News can project that Democrat Dr. Abdul El-Sayed will win his senate election against his Republican opponent, former Rep. Mike Rogers.

He will make history as this country’s first ever Muslim Senator. He faced consistent Islamophobic attacks from top Republicans, including the president.

El-Sayed consistently led in the polls, but faced a late challenge with Rep. Haley Steven's endorsement of Rogers on Sunday, but was able to rally the party around him in the closing days. His campaign focused on issues like Medicare for all and campaign finance reform.

item.title: Key part of Learjet broke off before deadly crash, but investigators don't know why
item.description:
FORT LAUDERDALE, Fla. — As federal investigators continue their probe of Sunday’s Learjet 60 crash in Palm Beach County amid rainy weather challenges, key pieces of evidence have been found, the National Transportation Safety Board announced Tuesday.

The jet’s left tail elevator was found in three pieces Monday within a range of 1.3 miles to 3.8 miles away from the site of impact on South Military Trail between Cresthaven Boulevard and 10th Avenue North, NTSB member Tom Chapman said at a news conference Tuesday afternoon.

The elevator controls the up and down pitch of the plane. Chapman did not have further details on exactly where the pieces were found but said they are being kept for analysis.

Shortly before 1 p.m. Sunday, the private business jet encountered bad weather and turbulence above Palm Beach County and nose-dived, violently crashing into a major road and gouging a large crater in some of the lanes. All nine people aboard were killed, among them co-pilot Nathalia Filgueiras, who attended West Boca High School when she earned her private pilot license at age 17.

The recovery of the elevator pieces is significant because it shows “some pieces of the aircraft, important pieces of the aircraft, separated before the impact,” Chapman said.

“What that means exactly, in terms of what caused the aircraft to lose control or whether the loss of this piece was a result of the forces on the aircraft — we don’t know yet … But finding that piece is a very, very significant bit of evidence,” he said at the news conference.

On Tuesday, public works teams were working with NTSB to drain water from the crater, and an unstable utility pole was removed from the site, which Chapman said will help investigators access and stabilize the area. Teams should be able to begin investigating in and around the crater Wednesday.

Chapman said he feels confident they will find “critical airplane components” within it, even while acknowledging it is a challenging site and that the aircraft pieces found in the crater are likely to be small.

Investigators on Tuesday were mainly focused on collecting and documenting wreckage, Chapman said. Evidence collected so far is “almost entirely very small pieces,” and investigators are largely unsure what the pieces that have been recovered even are, he said.

“We don’t know exactly what all we have yet, but that’s part of the investigation, very early here. It’s a big puzzle to try to put together,” Chapman said.

Hundreds of residents who live near the crash area are displaced and without a timeline for when they can return home, officials said Monday. Many live in a mobile home park that borders the crash site in Greenacres. Chapman on Tuesday said residents may soon have “limited access” in the area.

Military Trail between 10th Avenue North and Cresthaven Boulevard will remain closed until further notice, County Emergency Operations officials said in a news release Tuesday. Drivers are asked to use 10th Avenue North, Haverhill Road and Cresthaven Boulevard as detours.

Severe thunderstorms passed through the county Monday, complicating some aspects of the investigation, and the weather continues to be a “key challenge” Tuesday, Chapman said.

Some showers and storms are possible Wednesday in the county, with a 20% chance during the day, according to the National Weather Service Miami’s forecast. Thursday is forecast to be mostly clear.

Chapman urged community members who find pieces of wreckage to not touch or move the pieces and to contact the NTSB or local authorities.

item.title: 'I wasn't on the ballot': Trump distances himself from GOP midterm losses
item.description:
President Donald Trump sought to distance himself from Republicans' mounting midterm losses Tuesday, declaring in his first remarks on the election results that his party would have been victorious had he been on the ballot.

"I wasn’t on the Ballot and if I was, we would have won IN A LANDSLIDE!" Trump wrote on social media.

Trump's efforts to sidestep blame for the growing blue wave came as Republicans were dealt stunning losses in deep red states and districts, with Democrats flipping Senate seats in Texas, South Carolina, Kansas and Ohio. Republicans also lost Senate races in North Carolina and Georgia, and are trailing in other key contests.

Trump told the New York Times that he is "absolutely willing to accept" the election results.

“We’ll work with the Democrats, and we’ll, you know, look forward to working with them. We’ll probably work something out," Trump said.

Democrats are poised to flip both chambers of Congress by wide margins, with the party seizing on backlash to Trump's second-term agenda, including concerns about his handling of the economy and the Iran war.

Despite his record-low approval rating, Trump thrust himself into the center of the midterm election with a series of rallies across 20 states in the closing weeks.

The midterm contests are shaping up to be an emphatic repudiation of a president who implored voters to "pretend" he was on the ballot.

This article originally appeared on USA TODAY: 'I wasn't on the ballot': Trump distances himself from midterm results

item.title: Trump says U.S. is ready to strike Iran as negotiators struggle to reach deal
item.description:
By Parisa Hafezi and Jana Choukeir

DUBAI, Nov 3 (Reuters) - Iran and the United States are still far from a deal to end their war, a senior Iranian official told Reuters on Tuesday, as US President Donald Trump declined to rule out a resumption of US combat operations after the elections in the United States.

Trump made his comments in separate interviews as Americans voted in ‌pivotal midterm elections in which the unpopular Iran war has been a key factor and as mediator Qatar stepped up efforts to avert a renewed escalation.

Overnight, the United States carried out "defensive" strikes on Iran's ‌Qeshm island, targeting surface-to-air missiles used against US assets, a US official said. Another official said the strikes appeared limited and did not signal a return to major combat operations.

Trump on Tuesday renewed warnings of military action in an interview with the Fox News Channel. "I'm not looking ​to ... kill lots of people," he said. "If we have to, we'll have to."

In an interview with the Financial Times, Trump suggested he was content with the state of the stand-off with Iran.

"We seem to be getting everything we want," the paper quoted him as saying in a six-minute telephone interview.

The FT said it asked Trump about what it called "strong hints" by Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu that there would be an attack later this week.

"I’m ready, we’re ready. We’re locked and loaded if we need to go, but there may be no reason for it," he replied.

Trump told the FT indirect negotiations with Iran about its stockpile of enriched uranium were ongoing. "We’re having discussions, and we’ll see how that all works out," ‌he said.

Also on Tuesday, Trump made a surprise announcement of a deal with ⁠Netanyahu under which Washington would stop $4 billion in annual funding to Israel after this year, but would sell weapons to its close Middle East ally. The remarks appeared aimed at swaying voters unhappy with US support for Israel.

Fears have grown that the conflict launched by the United States and Israel in February could flare up again after Tuesday's midterms.

"Mediators are ⁠working hard to narrow gaps between Tehran and Washington," the senior Iranian official said, speaking on condition of anonymity. Qatari mediators travelled to Tehran on Monday night for talks on a version of a draft US-Iran deal discussed over the past eight days.

"Tehran's conditions must be met if the US wants Hormuz reopened," the Iranian official cautioned, referring to Iranian demands including waiving oil sanctions, ending the US naval blockade and releasing frozen Iranian funds.

Mohsen Rezaei, secretary of Iran's Supreme National Security Council, later said ​the ​US response to Iranian demands "was not convincing", adding that Washington "must fully and explicitly address Iran's seven conditions and act upon them".

"Only ​in this case will the Strait of Hormuz be reopened," he wrote on X.

'WE CANNOT ‌LOSE HOPE'

Qatar's foreign ministry spokesperson Majed al-Ansari said both the United States and Iran were reviewing proposals put forward by mediators. While the Qatari team that travelled to Tehran had returned to Doha, talks were continuing.

"There are intensive joint regional efforts underway to avoid escalation," he told a news briefing, adding that Qatar remained hopeful a deal could still be reached to pave the way for future negotiations.

"If there were no glimmer of hope, there would be no negotiations... and as a mediator, we cannot lose hope," he said.

An official briefed on the talks said feedback from Washington and Tehran was expected within the next 36 hours.

A senior Iranian official told Reuters later on Tuesday that there is no deadline for exchanging messages with Washington through mediators or reviewing responses.

'FORCEFUL RESPONSE'

The senior Iranian official said Tehran would not accept Washington's "excessive demands" and that nuclear talks could begin only after Iran's conditions were met.

Tehran would respond ‌forcefully, in the region and beyond, to US strikes, the official added.

Oil prices slipped in early trade on Wednesday as investors ​awaited the results of the midterm elections and their potential impact on peace talks, even after industry data showed US crude stocks unexpectedly ​fell last week.

Iran's Parliament Speaker Mohammad Baqer Qalibaf said the ball was in Washington's court after a "strong ​and rational response" from Tehran.

"The enemy seeks to force the Iranian nation into submission through threats and military action, but they are sorely mistaken; Iran will not submit," Qalibaf said. ‌He said Tehran's response to any US miscalculation would be unpredictable and unconstrained by ​geography.

The head of Iran's armed forces general staff, Ali Abdollahi, ​said Iran's military was updating target lists that included US and Israeli assets and would respond immediately to any threat.

Hardline newspaper Kayhan said on Tuesday that US facilities in Britain, Italy, Greece, Romania, Albania and Cyprus could be targeted in the event of renewed war.

IRANIAN-SAUDI TALKS

Alongside indirect exchanges between Tehran and Washington, regional powers are pursuing diplomatic efforts to prevent further escalation. The conflict has also widened, with Yemen's Iran-aligned ​Houthis stepping up attacks on Saudi Arabia.

Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araqchi said on Tuesday ‌talks with Saudi Arabia were continuing to seek new regional security arrangements that would exclude foreign military involvement.

Last week, senior officials from Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan met Iranian counterparts in Tehran, ​the first such high-level contacts since August.

(Additional reporting by Nayera Abdallah, Tala Ramadan and Elwely Elwelly in Dubai, Andrew Mills in Doha, Doina Chiacu and David Brunnstrom in Washington, Yasmine Ghania in ​Cairo; Writing by Dubai Newsroom and Tom Perry, Editing by Raju Gopalakrishnan, Ros Russell, Don Durfee and Kate Mayberry)

This article originally appeared on Reuters at https://uk.news.yahoo.com/irans-foreign-minister-says-talks-071254829.html

item.title: At least 124 people shot nationwide over Halloween weekend
item.description:
Violence at parties and other festivities marred the Halloween weekend, as police in multiple cities across the country investigated shootings and other mayhem that left at least 124 people shot, 17 fatally, authorities said.

"This is not normal," Delaware Gov. Matt Meyers said after shootings erupted at Halloween events in two cities in his state over the weekend. "We must never accept gun violence as part of life in Delaware."

Shootings occurred over the weekend at Halloween house parties and street parties in at least 15 cities, from California to Delaware, and the victims included a 5-year-old girl still in her Halloween costume, a pregnant woman and a college student, according to law enforcement officials. One shooting even occurred at a Halloween supply store.

15 shot, three fatally, in Chicago over Halloween weekend

The Chicago Police Department said officers responded to multiple shootings that left 15 people shot, three fatally.

Police said the victims who were killed included a 35-year-old man who was shot during an argument in the Mayfair neighborhood. One person of interest was taken into custody, police told ABC Chicago station WLS.

A 29-year-old man was killed and three others were shot in the North Lawndale neighborhood, when a two gunman exited a car and opened fire as the victims stood on a sidewalk.

A 41-year-old man died early Sunday after being shot and transporting himself to Holy Cross Hospital. No further information was released on the shooting.

2 shootings in Delaware leave girl dead and 8 other people wounded

The two shootings in Delaware happened on Saturday, Halloween night. One occurred at an outdoor Halloween party in Ellendale and left a 17-year-old girl dead and eight others wounded, according to the Ellendale Police Department.

"During an outdoor party, an unknown suspect allegedly opened fire from a neighboring property into a crowd, striking nine people," according to police.

No arrests have been announced.

The other shooting in Delaware occurred in Newark near the University of Delaware and left six people suffering from gunshot wounds, according to the Newark Police Department.

The shooting occurred on a sidewalk on East Main Street around 11:13 p.m. local time as hundreds of Halloween revelers were in the area.

Video obtained by ABC Philadelphia station WPVI showed people suddenly running for cover as the chaos unfolded.

One of the victims, a 20-year-old University of Delaware student, was hospitalized in serious condition with a bullet wound to the back and a collapsed lung, police said.

A 16-year-old boy who was wounded in the gunfire was arrested after police found he had a loaded firearm, authorities said.

The shooting prompted the University of Delaware to cancel classes on Monday and provide counseling to students traumatized by the incident, according to a university spokesperson.

1 dead, 6 injured in shooting at California Halloween store

A day before Halloween, a shooting at a Spirit Halloween store in Fairfield, California, left one person dead and six others injured, police said.

The shooting, which occurred around 8:30 p.m. local time, is believed to have stemmed from a targeted incident involving one suspect inside the Spirit Halloween store, police said in a statement Saturday.

The person killed was identified as Constance Hages, 31, who was pregnant at the time of her death, family members told police.

A 16-year-old boy, a 19-year-old man and a 32-year-old man were critically injured in the shooting, according to police. Three other men, ranging in age from 19 to 43, were also wounded in the incident, police said.

At a news conference on Monday afternoon, Fairfield police announced they had arrested a suspect in the shooting.

4 fatally shot in Dallas, 15 others injured in separate shootings

Dallas Police Chief Daniel Comeaux said three separate shootings occurred on Halloween night in the city's bustling Deep Ellum entertainment district.

Comeaux said four people were killed and 15 others were injured in the shootings despite beefed-up patrols in the neighborhood due to it being Halloween.

"This is completely unacceptable for this to take place in Dallas, and we're going to do everything we need to do to get everyone in custody who is responsible for this," Comeaux said during a news conference on Sunday.

He said officers were just two blocks away and heard the gunshots when the first shooting broke out.

He said one suspect is in custody as police work to find other assailants involved in the shootings.

7 shot at birthday party on Halloween in Edinburg, Texas

Seven people were hospitalized in shootings that happened at a birthday party on Halloween near Edinburg, Texas, the Hildalgo County Sheriff's Office told ABC affiliate station KRGC in Weslasco, Texas.

The shooting occurred around 11:45 p.m. at a home, police said.

"Upon arrival, deputies determined that an adult birthday party was taking place at the location," the sheriff’s office said in a statement. "Deputies located seven victims who had sustained gunshot wounds. The victims’ injuries were determined to be non-life-threatening."

5-year-old in Halloween costume shot in Detroit

Detroit police said they are investigating a shooting on Halloween night that left a 5-year-old girl, who was still in her Halloween costume, with a bullet wound to the chest.

The child was playing in a back room of her house after going trick-or-treating when she was struck by a gunshot fired from outside.

"For our victim, she was in her Halloween costume at the time she got shot," Detroit Deputy Police Chief Arnold Williams said during a news conference Saturday night.

Arnold said the child, who is in stable condition, cried out for her mother when she was shot.

"She had to tell her mom. She said, 'I think I've been shot.' The mom was in the shower and had to come down and rush her child here. This is just something senseless," Arnold said.

No arrests have been announced.

The incident marked the second shooting on Halloween in Michigan. In Flint, Michigan, a woman was killed and three other people were injured when gunfire broke out at a Halloween house party, according to the Flint Police Department.

Two juveniles and one adult were wounded in the shooting, police said.

No arrests have been made and a $2,500 reward is being offered in the case.

'Senseless': 7 shot at Halloween street celebration in Fayetteville

Gunfire erupted at a Halloween celebration in an entertainment district of Fayetteville, Arkansas, on Saturday night that left seven people shot, according to the Fayetteville Police Department.

In a statement, police described the shooting as a "random act of violence.

Fayetteville Mayor Molly Rawn said the shooting occurred near the Dickson Street entertainment district where up to 30,000 people were out celebrating Halloween.

"It was a senseless act of violence," Rawn said in a social media statement.

No arrests have been announced in the incident.

2 killed in Oklahoma City shooting at Halloween night get-together

In Oklahoma City, two people are killed and two others was injured after a shooting and vehicle crash involving pedestrians on Halloween night, according to the police.

"Responding officers found a chaotic scene that involved two deceased people under a car, and another lying near the scene with numerous gunshot wounds," the Oklahoma City Police Department said in a statement.

Investigators determined that all four victims were at a Halloween party when a fight broke out in a parking lot. Police said two men shot each other during the fight.

A 20-year-old woman, identified as Kyla Hysell, allegedly got into her car and "drove into the melee," hitting two people, who were both pronounced dead at the scene, police said.

Police identified the two people killed in the incident as Mayrah Torres and Isaac Lujan-Ochoa. Police said Torres and Lujan-Ochoa were both allegedly run over by Hysell and that Lujan-Ochoa was already deceased from the earlier shooting, according to police.

The man who was allegedly shot in the gunfight with Lujan-Ochoa was hospitalized in critical condition, police said. Hysell was arrested on charges of aggravated driving under the influence and felony murder, police said.

1 killed, 8 wounded in shooting after football game

One person was killed, and eight others were injured in a shooting after a football game in Birmingham, Alabama, on Halloween, law enforcement officials said.

At least one person was detained in connection with the shooting, according to the Birmingham Police Department.

Shortly after 7:50 p.m., multiple shots rang out near Legion Field, which earlier had hosted the Magic City Classic football game between Alabama A&M and Alabama State, according to police.

11 people shot in Jacksonville, Florida, 2 fatally, at Halloween events

In Jacksonville, Florida, police said 11 people were shot, two fatally, in separate incidents over the Halloween weekend.

A 17-year-old girl died after being shot while waiting to get into a Halloween party at a hotel in Jacksonville, according to police. Investigators believe the girl and two adults who were shot were innocent bystanders caught in the crossfire after an argument escalated into gunfire, according to police.

Another shooting in Jacksonville erupted hours later outside a Halloween house party that left a 20-year-old man dead and nine others, including a 15-year-old girl, injured, police said. No arrests have been made in either shooting.

1 killed, 8 wounded near Wesleyan University in Bloomington, Illinois

A 19-year-old woman was killed early Sunday when a shooting broke out at a Halloween party near the Wesleyan University campus in Bloomington, Illinois, according to police.

The shooting erupted around 1:23 a.m. on East Division Street and left other people wounded, according to police.

Officers were several blocks away patrolling the area when they heard gunshots, officials said.

The wounded victims included individuals affiliated with Wesleyan University and Illinois State University, police said.

No arrests were immediately announced.

7 injured in shooting near Indiana University on Halloween

Seven people, ranging in age from 17 to 27, were wounded when gunfire broke out early Sunday morning near Indiana University in Bloomington, Indiana, police said.

"None of the injured individuals are believed to be students at Indiana University, and those that provided statements to detectives stated they had come to Bloomington to party and celebrate Halloween," Bloomington Deputy Police Chief Ryan Pedigo told reporters.

Pedigo said one gun was found at the scene of the shooting and a person was taken into custody. No charges have been announced.

Bloomington Mayor Kerry Thomson said in a video statement on Sunday that all seven victims were in stable condition and that police had arrested a suspect.

"Gun violence has visited a Bloomington celebration once again and we should all be angry. I know I am," Thompson said.

3 juveniles among 4 shot at Nashville Halloween street party

Four people, including three juveniles, were shot around 12:25 a.m. local time on Sunday during a Halloween street party in Nashville, Tennessee, according to the Nashville Police Department.

One of the victims was a 16-year-old girl, who was critically injured, police said. A 14-year-old boy and a 15-year-old boy, along with an 18-year-old male, were also shot in the incident, police said.

Police said some of the shots were fired from a passing vehicle.

No arrests were announced.

University of Colorado student killed in shooting at Halloween party

In Boulder, Colorado, two students from the University of Colorado were shot, one fatally, at a Halloween house party on Saturday in an area known as The Hill near the university, according to the Boulder Police Department.

The University of Colorado Boulder announced Monday evening that the student who was shot and killed on Saturday was 19-year-old Luca Hanlon, a second-year media production student.

On Monday, Boulder police said 18-year-old Omar Perez of Thornton, Colorado, was arrested on Monday morning and charged with first-degree murder with extreme indifference and assault in the first-degree with extreme indifference.

This article originally appeared on ABC News at https://abcnews.com/US/halloween-shootings-nation-left-17-people-dead-86/story?id=137765951
